title: Hand washes hand
hookLine: what makes a true brahmin? virtue and wisdom, each washing the other like two hands
carry: where one is, the other is
last: NO TALK OF BIRTH AT THE SUMMIT.

cards: Sonadanda is a distinguished brahmin of the city of Campa, living on land granted by the king. When the Buddha arrives, Sonadanda decides to go and see him. On the way, the text says, he starts to worry.
What if I ask a question and he says it's not the right question? What if he asks me something and I can't answer? Everyone will see, and my reputation will suffer.
It's a very human fear: looking foolish in public. The Buddha, reading his mind, asks him about his own subject.

teach.b: What makes someone a true brahmin? Sonadanda relaxes and lists five things. Good birth on both sides for seven generations.
Mastery of the Vedic verses. Good looks. Virtue.
And wisdom. Could one be left out? Yes: looks.
Another? Yes, the verses. And another?
Yes, even birth. The other brahmins are shocked. Don't say that!
Sonadanda points at his own nephew, sitting right there: handsome, learned, well born. But if he killed, stole, went with other men's wives, lied, and drank, what would all that be worth?
Virtue and wisdom are what make a brahmin. Could one of those two be dropped? No.
And then he says the line that names the day.
Wisdom is purified by virtue, and virtue is purified by wisdom. Where one is, the other is.
As one hand washes the other, as one foot washes the other. The Buddha agrees: that's how it is, brahmin. The Pali words are sila and pañña: virtue and wisdom.
Notice who says the line. Not the Buddha.
Sonadanda, the brahmin, speaking from his own tradition; the Buddha just keeps asking until it's said. And the ending is honest about people. Sonadanda goes for refuge, but asks a favor.
If I meet you in public and raise my joined hands, take it as standing up. If I take off my turban, take it as bowing. My reputation, you see.
Even after all that, he's still a little worried about looking foolish.

how: Buddhist teaching across schools holds virtue and wisdom together, with concentration, as the three trainings; some teachers cite Sonadanda's image of two hands washing each other to show that neither is complete alone.

o: good birth on both sides of a family
a brahmin's mastery of the verses

games.q: hand washes hand: tap the pairs.
p: handsome and learned, but if he harmed?
stand-in for rising from his seat

s: the Buddha himself says the line about two hands washing
Sonadanda says it, from his own tradition; the Buddha agrees.
Sonadanda agrees that even birth can be left out
pointing to his own nephew, he says virtue and wisdom are what count.
after going for refuge, Sonadanda stops caring about his reputation entirely
he asks the Buddha to take a raised hand or a lifted turban as a bow in public.

games.q: the Buddha asks Sonadanda: of the five qualities of a brahmin, can one be left out? what does Sonadanda drop first?
games.why: he drops looks, then the verses, then birth, and holds on to virtue and wisdom, which he says wash each other like two hands.

practice: Picture washing your hands slowly: water running, one hand rubbing the other, then the other rubbing back, neither doing it alone.
Let one hand be what you know and the other how you act, and feel them cleaning each other, then rest your hands in your lap and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Pañña. Wisdom, purified by virtue as virtue is purified in turn; where one is, the other is.

orig.note: Pali pañña (Sanskrit prajña): wisdom, understanding. washed by virtue, and washing it in turn.

carryVoice: Your line: where one is, the other is. Knowing and doing, each washing the other. That's day five hundred thirty-three.
